documents.abstract: Push notifications can do more than promote a single merchant: They can redirect attention across an entire mobile marketplace. Drawing on more than 200 campaigns, 60 million user-campaign observations, and two controlled experiments, this study shows that notifications substantially increase same-day engagement with advertised merchants while also generating meaningful spillovers to other merchants within and across categories. Effectiveness varies by merchant, user, message design, and delivery timing. Notifications tend to work especially well for less prominent merchants, newer users, Android users, deeper discounts, urgency cues, and carefully timed delivery. However, repeated exposure produces diminishing returns and can eventually reduce engagement as annoyance and attentional overload increase. For platform managers, the findings support managing notifications as a portfolio rather than evaluating campaigns in isolation: targeting, message design, timing, cross-merchant benefits, and cumulative frequency should be optimized jointly. Platforms should also incorporate spillover value into campaign pricing, performance reporting, and merchant communication. For policymakers and platform-governance leaders, the results underscore the importance of meaningful consent, frequency controls, and transparent notification practices that protect user attention while preserving the economic benefits of timely, relevant mobile communication.

Abstract The rapid expansion of data center infrastructure, accelerated by the growing computational demands of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), has led to an unprecedented increase in electricity consumption. As AI developers race to deploy GenAI products, time-to-market pressure drives continuous model training that demands baseload power, often from high-CO 2 emissions sources like natural gas and coal instead of intermittent renewables like wind and solar. Carbon-aware strategies that shift model training in real time to periods or locations with cleaner power on the margin have emerged as a near-term decarbonization lever, but the relative effectiveness of temporal flexibility (pausing model training during high-carbon hours) versus spatial flexibility (migrating workloads to cleaner grid regions) remains poorly understood under real-world constraints. This study evaluates these strategies using 2025 marginal operating CO 2 emissions rate (MOER) data from WattTime across 43 subregions spanning four US grid operators: California Independent System Operator (CAISO), Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), Midcontinent Independent System Operator, and Pennsylvania–Jersey–Maryland (PJM). Using Meta’s LLaMA 3.1 model family as representative workloads, we simulate four scenarios: business-as-usual, reflecting a carbon-informed siting choice with no real-time operational flexibility (S1, BAU); temporal flexibility with varying pause thresholds (S2); ideal spatial flexibility (S3); and spatial flexibility incorporating migration overhead (S4). We find that effective strategies are grid-dependent. In grids with high subregional MOER heterogeneity, spatial flexibility dominates: ERCOT achieves up to 36% emissions reduction via intraday alternation between wind-rich and solar-heavy zones, and the inter-ISO configuration achieves 67.3% reduction, with CAISO and ERCOT absorbing over 80% of training hours. In PJM, where subregional MOER profiles are largely homogeneous, spatial flexibility achieves only 0.3% emissions reduction while temporal flexibility reduces emissions by up to 17.2% relative to S1. The emissions-training time tradeoff under temporal flexibility is nonlinear: moderate reductions require marginal increases in training time, but near-zero emissions require nearly four times the baseline training duration. These findings provide grid-specific guidance for developers pursuing near-term decarbonization, and highlight opportunities for further improvement through empirical characterization of data migration overhead.

Detecting novelty remains a persistent weakness of modern artificial intelligence (AI): systems that achieve impressive in-distribution accuracy can still fail under distribution shift, open-set conditions, and embodied settings where self-generated sensory changes confound external events. Nervous systems face closely related problems under tight constraints of latency, memory, and continual adaptation, suggesting that brain-inspired mechanisms may offer useful design principles rather than metaphors. This article reviews progress on two computational scenarios linking cerebellum and cerebellum-like circuits to novelty-related functions. The first, prediction–cancellation, learns sensory expectations from motor commands, state, context, and multimodal feedback, and subtracts predictable components via negative images, adaptive filtering, or internal forward models so that unpredicted external inputs emerge as residual signals. The second, high-dimensional expansion, transforms inputs into sparse, high-dimensional codes that alter similarity structure, reduce interference, and increase capacity; novelty and familiarity—along with set membership and frequency—can then be computed by plastic readouts. Although both scenarios can yield novelty-related signals, they define “novelty” differently and depend on different learning targets. Studies of the cerebellum proper most directly support prediction and residual coding of unexpected self-motion, whereas explicit memory-based novelty and familiarity readouts have been demonstrated most clearly in the Drosophila mushroom body. Finally, we connect these circuit-level ideas to recent AI algorithms and propose an explicitly conceptual model that integrates expansion coding with multi-timescale plasticity to support fast detection, short-term adaptation, and longer-term incorporation of persistent changes.

Background We developed a hospital web application that searches 266 destinations and links results to indoor navigation. Its default retrieval tiers run locally; an optional cloud large language model (LLM) tier requires explicit invocation. Synthetic queries were used because default-tier searches are not server-logged. Objective We examined how post hoc review of an LLM-generated benchmark changed the apparent benefit of completed system updates. Methods Version v2 added pronunciation aliases to v1; v3 added colloquial knowledge, pronunciation forms, destination-level score combination, and false-match rules. Two v3 rules were informed by evaluation-query failures. A clinician and a medical administrative coauthor jointly reviewed 563 synthetic queries without blinding, excluding 129 and rewriting 289 under review-defined policies. The final data contained 401 answerable and 33 no-valid-destination queries. Archived versions were compared across sequential review stages and with lexical and embedding implementations. Results Among the same 192 answerable evaluation-query identifiers and final accepted destinations, rewriting increased top-1 accuracy from 43.8% to 62.0% for v1 and from 56.8% to 63.0% for v3. Their difference remained near 13 percentage points through earlier review stages and decreased to 1.0 point at rewriting. The tested multilingual-E5-small implementation achieved higher top-3 accuracy than v3 (87.0% vs. 69.3%; exploratory P < 0.001), with differences in passage scoring, abstention, and evidence display. For v3, candidate returns occurred on 4/11 reviewed no-valid-destination evaluation queries and 11/29 original queries in a retrospective sensitivity analysis. Conclusions Unblinded benchmark editing changed performance estimates for frozen systems within this synthetic corpus. The findings do not establish improved real-user performance, independent generalization, or comparative clinical safety. The version difference is conditional on the review intervention; neither wording distribution was validated against patient input. Review before optimization and independent user evaluation require prospective assessment.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly being explored as assistants for chemistry instructors, including the preparation of teaching materials. Here, we examined whether ChatGPT, using Images 2.0, can generate scientifically correct images for first-year undergraduate chemistry students, focusing on visual and symbolic representations central to the discipline. A total of 444 images covering six chemistry areas were generated. Short, minimally descriptive prompts were used first; when important errors appeared, more detailed corrective prompts were introduced. We also generated instructional infographics combining several representations to explain chemical concepts. Scientific accuracy depended strongly on image complexity, with simpler orbitals, titration curves, and molecular structures generally performing better than more demanding examples. When the six categories were equally weighted, 43.5% of basic-prompt images, 45.6% of images from corrective prompts, and only 8.3% of instructional infographics were directly usable. Embedded text was generally more accurate than the images. Expert checking therefore remains essential before classroom use.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The Global Digital Compact, adopted by Member States in September 2024 as an annex to the Pact for the Future, sets shared objectives on digital divides, the digital economy, human rights online, data governance and the international governance of artificial intelligence. Whether those commitments matter depends on what happens in cities, where public services, infrastructure and community life meet digital systems. This paper argues that a city-level deployment of sovereign artificial intelligence is a valid and auditable target for the Compact's localisation, provided that democratic agency is written into the protocols that govern the system rather than left outside them. It brings together four bodies of work developed across a single line of inquiry. First, the topology of city-level AI: governance under Permanent Systemic Instability shifts from territorial monopoly to Flow Sovereignty, the maintenance of coherent, low-surprise trajectories across digital, physical and financial systems, organised through active inference, information-geometric policy navigation, sheaf-theoretic consensus and a 72-hour autonomy standard. Second, the Digital Agora, the rights-based counter-model to the Algorithmic Leviathan, which relocates democratic constraints from the political layer to the protocol layer. Third, the primitives that make such constraints enforceable: layered Sybil resistance, quadratic weighting of preference intensity, and the Minimal Anti-Collusion Infrastructure (MACI), which makes votes private, receipt-free and publicly tallied. Fourth, the cryptographic foundations of verification: zk-SNARKs, the per-circuit trusted setup of Groth16, the universal and updatable setup of PLONK, and Kate–Zaverucha–Goldberg polynomial commitments. The paper composes these into a six-layer deployment architecture, maps it to the Compact's five objectives, states five validity criteria a city deployment must meet, and sets out a pilot programme whose outputs are the local evidence the Compact asks for. It also states the limits: residual trust in setups and coordinators, the trade-off between Sybil resistance and inclusion, prover cost at city scale, and the sovereignty trap of new external dependencies. The work is a design specification; its single computation is an analytic illustration and contains no empirical data. KSCCN article prepared in connection with the GDC Localization Townhall, "Localizing the Global Digital Compact: From global frameworks to local implementation" (UN Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies, 18 November 2026). Companion to "City-Level AI: The Topology of Command and Information Geometry (Volume II)" (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22990597) and "The Algorithmic Leviathan" (Volume I, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22990607). documents.abstract: Research impact quantification plays a crucial role in academic assessment. Conventional citation-based metrics have several limitations in fair and comprehensive research evaluation. They often fail to recognize foundational work that receives limited early attention. They may also overlook sustained influence over time, differences across research fields, citation quality reflected by citation contexts and the expertise of citing authors, and variations in author contributions. We incorporate these aspects at the paper level through four factors: originality-oriented downstream influence, long-term influence, field-specific ranking, and citation quality. At the researcher level, we quantify credit according to author order. Based on these, we propose CLOF, a unified metric framework that quantifies the impacts of papers and researchers in an interdependent and iterative manner. To reduce reliance on manually specified weighting schemes, we employ multiple large language model (LLM)-based paper scorers. Their outputs are aggregated using an α-trimmed procedure to generate robust global signals for learning the combination weights. These learned weights further guide the coupled iterative updates of paper and researcher scores via a Double Iterative Power (DIP) method with theoretical convergence guarantees. Extensive experiments on academic datasets show that CLOF uncovers influence patterns across papers and researchers that are not captured by existing impact metrics.

Background/Objectives: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurodegenerative disease affecting the central nervous system and significantly reducing the quality of life. Early detection of the disease is critical for slowing its progression and developing appropriate treatment plans. In recent years, artificial intelligence and deep learning methods have begun to play a significant role in clinical decision support systems, particularly due to their high accuracy rates in the analysis of Magnetic Resonance (MR) images. Methods: In this study, a hybrid model was developed for the automatic classification of MS. Two different architectures were used for feature extraction in the developed model. These architectures were selected from among the most successful architectures out of 10 different Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures. Six different classifiers were used to classify the feature maps obtained in the proposed model and pre-trained models. The application of the VOTE operation in the final stage of the proposed model improved its performance. Results: The proposed model yielded competitive results compared to similar studies in the literature and the CNN and ViT architectures used in this study. The accuracy rate achieved with the proposed hybrid model was 97.28%. Conclusions: These results indicate that the proposed model has the potential to support computer-aided MS detection and may provide a useful framework for clinical decision support systems.

Understanding human cognitive processes for reasoning is a key step towards developing human-level AI reasoning systems. Syllogistic reasoning — a classical form of deductive reasoning — is a well-established paradigm for investigating human reasoning, known to elicit systematic cognitive biases such as belief bias and atmosphere effects. In this study, we compare the reasoning patterns of humans and three state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs), namely GPT-4, GPT-4o and o4-mini, across multiple syllogism types with belief andatmosphere effects. Using an online questionnaire, we examine the biases in human syllogistic reasoning and compare this with the LLMs responses. We identify biases and differences in accuracy between different LLMs and humans. Belief-inconsistent statements, which contradict generally accepted common knowledge, and the atmosphere effect impact human and LLM answers. Our results show that, although LLMs outperform human participants, they exhibit human-like cognitive effects. We further evaluate the new reasoning model o4-mini, which performs nearly perfectly on the syllogism reasoning tasks and compare logic, human reasoning and LLM reasoning.

Remote ship operation involves analysing information from various perspectives. However, a standardized educational approach for training remote ship operators is lacking. This study addresses the challenges posed by the cognitive attributes of individuals using remote ship operation and monitoring systems by investigating how different perspectives (first-vs. third-person) impact skill acquisition in ship operation. It introduces the ‘cognitive approach limit circle’ (CLC) concept, a decision-making criterion in ship operation, and formulate two hypotheses. The study conducted repeated ship operation trials from both perspectives in congested traffic scenarios over 100 iterations, analysing the learning trajectory regarding safety and efficiency. Accordingly, mitigating safety and efficiency inclination differences between perspectives is challenging. However, repeated exposure to ship operation experiences facilitates the acquisition of safety and efficiency skills that align with the cognitive attributes of the information utilized. Therefore, in training remote ship operators, initial emphasis on collision avoidance through exercises based on qualitative perceptual data—such as object orientation changes and distance perceived directly through retinal image alterations—rather than quantitative computer-generated information promotes the development of CLC awareness tailored to individual capabilities.

How people imagine the future of artificial intelligence (AI) can play a significant role in shaping the development and use of AI. This study investigates collective future thinking about AI in emerging adults and factors that may influence the valence of the imagined events. Participants (N = 158) were asked to imagine, within 1 minute, as many worrying or exciting events about AI as they could that might happen in the near or distant futures. They also completed measures for their attitudes toward AI, technological readiness, and political ideology. Results showed that participants generated more worrying than exciting events for both near and distant futures. The worrying events primarily concerned ethical issues, unemployment, negative cognitive consequences of reliance on AI, and threats to humankind. Exciting events primarily involved scientific breakthroughs, increased efficiency, and assistance with learning, cognition, and well-being. Moreover, the more positive participants felt about AI and general technology, the more exciting relative to worrying events they imagined. Also, participants who self-identified as more conservative imagined more exciting relative to worrying events than those who self-identified as more liberal, and women imagined more worrying events than men. These original findings provide insights into the anticipatory process regarding AI and have societal implications for AI development and use.

documents.abstract: Abstract This study investigates whether LLM-based Conversational Agents (LLMCAs) could be employed as assistive technologies, helping anyone navigate a website by explaining its content and interactive features, and suggesting actions to accomplish specific goals. This would make the web more accessible especially to seniors, blind users and people with mild cognitive impairment. Specifically, the study examines whether such tools can analyze the source code of a webpage to identify its structure and interactive elements, understand which interactive components are required to support users in achieving their goals, and act effectively as assistive technologies. In addition, the work compares leading tools to assess differences in their effectiveness and behavior in supporting accessible web interaction. The work presents two empirical studies in which four popular LLMCA tools are evaluated on a set of public websites, in order to assess their ability to understand web page structures and interactive components and assist users in their tasks. The evaluation combines qualitative and quantitative measures, focusing on accuracy, completeness, and practical usefulness of the responses.Results show a good degree of pertinent and good-quality answers, even on websites with a poorly accessible structure. The user-friendly way to interact with a LLMCA makes it much comfortable to use for the average user. However, the study also highlights that some LLMCAs appear more 'skilled' in accessibility tasks than others. LLMCAs show promising potential not only to complement existing assistive technologies but also to support or replace the human assistance that is often required for many users to effectively access the web.

documents.abstract: Background Patients and caregivers increasingly rely on LLMs for health information, yet their performance in TT, a time-critical urological emergency, remains insufficiently characterized. This study compared three LLMs across content safety, quality, reliability, readability, understandability, and actionability. Methods Twenty-five standardized patient-centered questions were developed based on clinical guidelines, expert consensus documents, and information needs identified through Google Trends. Each question was submitted to GPT-5.6 Sol (High reasoning mode), DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and Doubao 2.0 Expert Model, yielding 75 responses. Quality and reliability were assessed using GQS, mDISCERN, and QAMAI; understandability and actionability were evaluated using PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A, respectively. Readability was assessed using six English-language indices, and content deficiencies were also evaluated. Results GPT-5.6 Sol(High reasoning mode) achieved significantly higher GQS, mDISCERN, and QAMAI scores than the other two models (all overall P < 0.001). Hallucinations and factual inaccuracies occurred in 28.0% and 17.3% of responses, respectively. No hallucinations were detected in GPT-5.6 Sol responses, compared with 44.0% for DeepSeek-V4-Pro and 40.0% for Doubao 2.0 Expert Model. Understandability did not differ significantly among models ( P = 0.0735), whereas actionability did ( P < 0.001), with GPT-5.6 Sol(High reasoning mode) performing best. All six readability indices differed significantly among models (all P < 0.001). DeepSeek-V4-Pro showed the most favorable relative readability, GPT-5.6 Sol(High reasoning mode) intermediate performance, and Doubao 2.0 Expert Model the greatest reading difficulty. Conclusions The three LLMs exhibited distinct performance profiles in generating TT-related health information. GPT-5.6 Sol (High reasoning mode) achieved the highest scores for quality, reliability, and actionability, whereas DeepSeek-V4-Pro showed comparatively better readability. Understandability did not differ significantly among models. However, hallucinations, factual inaccuracies, and substantial reading demands remain concerns. These findings reflect model performance under the specific evaluation conditions and at the time of data collection, rather than established clinical effectiveness or safety. GPT-5.6 Sol(High reasoning mode) may be the most suitable supplementary information tool among the models evaluated, but it should not replace professional medical assessment or clinical decision-making.

documents.abstract: Abstract Attentional distraction is an established strategy for reducing acute pain, yet relatively few studies have examined the psychophysiological correlates of gamified biofeedback interventions. This pilot study investigated whether gamified biofeedback tasks can modulate subjective and physiological responses to acute pain. Twenty healthy adults participated in a within-subject experiment consisting of three successive pain conditions, induced by the Cold Pressor Test. The first trial used no intervention, followed by two gamified intervention conditions, presented in a counterbalanced order across participants. One used electrodermal activity (EDA) biofeedback with the Calm The Waves (CTW) system; the other used a visual search task designed to induce cognitive load. Seven participants had prior training in the CTW task (experts). Subjective pain intensity was assessed using a Numeric Rating Scale (NRS), and EDA was continuously recorded throughout each two-minute trial. Mixed-design repeated-measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were conducted to examine the effects of condition and prior CTW training. Subjective pain ratings differed significantly across pain conditions, F (2, 36) = 11.41, p < .001, ηp² = .388. Pain baseline M = 6.80 (1.10), pain with CTW M = 6.30 (1.90) and pain with Visual Task M = 5.40 (1.70). In contrast, mean EDA did not differ significantly across conditions, nor across participants’ expertise status. These findings suggest that gamified interventions are associated with reduced subjective pain during acute pain exposure, while corresponding changes in average electrodermal activity were not evident. Both real-time physiological biofeedback and sustained cognitive engagement may contribute to acute pain modulation, although further research is needed to determine whether these effects translate into broader self-regulation skills. Future studies with larger samples and clinical populations should investigate whether dynamic EDA measures are more sensitive indicators of physiological changes associated with acute pain. These findings may contribute to the refinement of biofeedback training approaches for acute pain modulation.

Diagnosing root fractures, especially vertical root fractures (VRFs), is one of the most difficult diagnostic issues in endodontics. Despite the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in radiograph interpretation, no pooled diagnostic-accuracy estimates have existed for this question. The aim was to systematically review and meta-analyze the diagnostic accuracy of AI for detecting root fractures across cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), periapical, and panoramic radiography. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, Embase, and IEEE Xplore were searched from the date of inception to June 2026 (PROSPERO CRD420251121564). Eligible studies used AI to diagnose root fracture with extractable 2×2 diagnostic data. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were derived using a bivariate random-effects model with the hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) modeling. Thirteen studies (2013-2026) were synthesized qualitatively; three (576 fractured, 576 non-fractured teeth) contributed to the meta-analysis. Pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.90-0.97), and pooled specificity was 0.97 (95% CI: 0.77-1.00). Heterogeneity was substantial for sensitivity (I²=77.9%) and specificity (I²=95.6%), driven largely by one outlying study. The summary point approximated the ideal upper-left corner of SROC space. Certainty of evidence was moderate. AI demonstrated excellent pooled diagnostic accuracy for root-fracture detection, with CBCT-based deep learning models performing best. However, substantial heterogeneity and risk-of-bias concerns temper confidence, pending larger, prospective, externally validated studies.

documents.abstract: Rebound tonometry is widely used for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP) in cats; however, differences in clinical tonometer measurement configuration may contribute to variability in recorded values. This prospective repeated-measures study compared IOP measurements obtained using horizontal and vertical Tonovet Plus clinical measurement configurations in 32 client-owned, systemically and ophthalmologically normal conscious cats. Intraocular pressure was measured in the right eye while the probe was directed toward the center of the cornea and positioned 4-8 mm from the corneal surface. The order of horizontal and vertical configurations was randomized for each cat. Measurements were obtained by one experienced veterinary ophthalmologist and a trained student operator group. In the primary linear mixed-effects analysis accounting for repeated measurements within cats, horizontal configuration was associated with an estimated 2.41-mmHg higher IOP than vertical configuration (β = 2.41 mmHg; 95% CI, 1.39-3.44; p < 0.001). The configuration-associated difference was also observed separately for the experienced instructor (mean difference, 2.81 mmHg; 95% CI, 1.91-3.71; p < 0.001) and across the trained student operator group (2.00 mmHg; 95% CI, 0.81-3.19; p = 0.002). These findings indicate that horizontal and vertical Tonovet Plus clinical measurement configurations may yield different IOP values in conscious cats. As configuration changes may affect instrument handling, restraint, head positioning, and animal responses, the difference cannot be attributed solely to tonometer orientation or mechanics. Consistent configuration is therefore recommended when comparing serial IOP measurements in cats. Further controlled studies are needed to distinguish mechanical, ergonomic, and other examination-related mechanisms.

The rapid advancement of AI-assisted software engineering has brought transformative potential to the field of software engineering, but existing tools and paradigms remain limited by cognitive overload, inefficient tool integration, and the narrow capabilities of AI copilots. In response, we propose Compiler.next , a novel search-based compiler designed to enable the seamless evolution of AI-native software systems as part of the emerging Software Engineering 3.0 era. Unlike traditional static compilers, Compiler.next takes human-written intents and automatically generates working software by searching for an optimal solution. This process involves dynamic optimization of cognitive architectures and their constituents (e.g., prompts, foundation model configurations, and system parameters) while finding the optimal tradeoff between several objectives, such as accuracy, cost, and latency. This article outlines the architecture of Compiler.next and positions it as a cornerstone in democratizing software development by lowering the technical barrier for non-experts, enabling scalable, adaptable, and reliable AI-powered software. We present a roadmap to address the core challenges in intent compilation, including developing quality programming constructs, effective search heuristics, reproducibility, and interoperability between compilers. Our vision lays the groundwork for fully automated, search-driven software development, fostering faster innovation and more efficient AI-driven systems.

Abstract Across living organisms, eusocial superorganisms, human social networks, imperial bureaucracies, financial clearing systems, frontier artificial intelligence architectures, and technological civilizations on cosmic timescales, complex systems exhibit an invariant structural failure signature: they rarely collapse when visibly depleted, instead stalling, oscillating, and fracturing at apparent peak scale. This monograph formalizes Complexity and Information Compression Dynamics (CICD) as a substrate-invariant theoretical framework governing the joint evolution of structural coordination overhead and cross-boundary information compression. Every bounded system operates on a finite flux of gross capacity (E_gross) partitioned between internal maintenance and coordination overhead (E_maint) and net discretionary surplus (E_net). Because relational interdependencies scale super-linearly with effective structural dimensionality (C), every non-modular topology encounters a hard thermodynamic ceiling—the Complexity Maximum (C_max)—where internal upkeep consumes total capacity (E_net → 0). Simultaneously, transmitting high-dimensional internal states across finite-bandwidth internal or external interfaces (B_int) requires lossy compression, elevating the dimensionless Information Compression Friction Index (Φ ≥ 1) above the Landauer–Shannon thermodynamic floor and inflicting structural fidelity loss (ΔΨ). By the Two-Way Coupling Lemma (C ↔ Φ), rising complexity degrades cross-boundary legibility past a Legibility Horizon, while compression reconciliation overhead consumes discretionary surplus and contracts the effective Complexity Maximum downward. When complexity saturation (σ = C / C_max) converges with lossy compression lag, systemic damping vanishes at a critical Hopf bifurcation threshold (σ_crit), inducing Pre-Collapse Oscillatory Judder, pre-critical shock amplification (Λ(σ)), post-critical exponential runaway, and structural epistemic blindness—forcing either a deliberate topological phase-jump behind low-entropy symbolic interfaces or violent involuntary complexity shedding. From these four foundational axioms, the monograph derives four formal corollaries spanning the complete physical phase diagram of bounded scaling—Thermodynamic Fitness Traps, Low-Entropy Interface Kill Switches, Conjugate Compression–Compute Conservation, and the High-Latency Monolith Prohibition—and validates the framework across thirty orders of magnitude in scale. These derivations resolve apparent anomalies ranging from the two-billion-year prokaryotic plateau, eusocial ant-mill cascades, crocodilian ectothermic stasis and somatic-repair energetics, beaver externalized compute loops, sleep as an offline Regime 2 reset, human qualia as a 20-watt executive compression codec, and Homo sapiens as the sole surviving hominin species, to pre-modern imperial fragmentation, the July 1914 European mobilization cascade, the ~4 GHz multi-core microprocessor frequency wall, post-transformer artificial intelligence architectures, and the Fermi Paradox, concluding with a zero-free-parameter empirical falsification protocol. · Authorial & Computational Disclosure: The theoretical framework, core axioms, cross-scale synthesis, and structural direction of this monograph were conceived, directed, and validated by the author. Large language model computational assistance was used to aid in drafting the prose, formalize the mathematical derivations, and perform structural verification under the author's continuous instruction and editorial control.

Digital Twin technologies in maritime applications have primarily focused on individual subsystems, such as vessel machinery, navigation, or environmental monitoring, while limited attention has been given to the integrated representation of human operators, vessel dynamics, machinery, and environmental conditions. To address this challenge, a conceptual Virtual Symbiotic Environment for Maritime Operations (VSEMO) is proposed; the VSEMO integrates human, traffic, docking, environmental, and machinery Digital Twins within a closed-loop system engineering framework. The proposed architecture incorporates Explainable Artificial Intelligence to support transparent operational risk assessment and decision support, while immersive virtual reality provides a realistic environment for adaptive operator training. As an initial proof of concept, a Graph Convolutional Network is developed using synthetic graph-based operational scenarios to demonstrate the feasibility of jointly estimating subsystem-level and aggregate operational risk indicators. Although the computational implementation is limited to snapshot-based synthetic data, the proposed framework establishes a scalable and modular foundation for future real-time Digital Twin ecosystems that integrate physiological sensing, vessel telemetry, environmental information, and explainable artificial intelligence for maritime training and decision support.

Technologies can themselves become objects of stigmatization, rather than merely serving as vehicles through which stigma is directed at associated individuals or organizations. As technologies evolve, shifts in their benefits and harms may alter the grounds for stigma. Yet it remains unclear how these shifts shape stigma trajectories. We examine this issue through a longitudinal qualitative study of the stigmatization of internal combustion engine (ICE) scooters in Taiwan (2009–2021), a case in which a proposal to phase them out in favor of electric scooters was later withdrawn. We show how stigmatizing and stigmatized audiences, evolving technologies, and infrastructures co-constitute evaluative conditions that shape which attributes and consequences acquire discrediting significance. Stigma first attached to legacy ICE models and then spread to all ICE scooters. Its scope later narrowed as upgraded variants regained acceptance, although legacy models remained discredited. This oscillating trajectory unfolds through three mechanisms: constituting a graded technological order, polarizing this order, and reconstituting technological normality. Our model thus extends audience-centered accounts by explaining how human and nonhuman elements jointly shape the trajectory and scope of technology stigma.

Catalysis is central to energy conversion and green chemistry, but its development is constrained by fragmented literature data, complex reaction systems, difficult mechanistic identification, and reliance on empirical trial and error. Large language models (LLMs), with capabilities in unstructured text understanding, multisource knowledge integration, reasoning, and tool invocation, have been increasingly applied to literature extraction, characterization analysis, mechanistic hypothesis generation, catalyst recommendation, condition optimization, and automated experimentation. However, catalytic tasks are highly specialized, condition-dependent, and validation-intensive, making general-purpose LLMs insufficient for traceable, verifiable, safe, and controllable research. This review summarizes recent progress in applying LLMs to key catalytic tasks and discusses their reliability requirements. We further propose a catalysis-oriented vertical LLM framework consisting of "task definition-evidence access-constraint control-model adaptation-validation evaluation-feedback updating." By integrating evidence-constrained knowledge extraction, constraint-aware decision-making, and feedback-driven closed-loop optimization, this framework aims to reduce low-value trial-and-error experiments, unnecessary reagent consumption, energy input, and waste generation, thereby supporting reliable and sustainable catalysis research.

Abstract The current development of artificial intelligence (AI) is sustained by powerful imaginaries that describe possible technological futures aligning with the normative preferences of influential actors. We show how an AI imaginary driven by “Big Tech” corporate interests and technosolutionism has influenced the development of an AI/cybersecurity imaginary in the UK. Building on the Science and Technology Studies concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, we adopt atechnopolitical lens to examine how external notions of AI progress and development interacted with internal U.K. government commitments to cybersecurity. Drawing on U.K. government texts and interviews with 37 officials, nongovernment experts, and industry actors, we trace the emergence of an AI/cybersecurity imaginary between 2022 and 2024, how intragovernment controversies were negotiated and resolved, and how this imaginary stabilised in U.K. security politics with identifiable outcomes in cybersecurity governance. The article contributes empirical support for the importance of sociotechnical imaginaries in understanding security trajectories, how corporate and technosolutionist imaginaries influence government policy and practice, and offer theoretical insights into the dynamics of imaginary formation and function. AI imaginaries promote the goals and values of science and technology, while technopolitics dominated by corporate actors and technoscientific optimism constrain governmental and social capacity to create and enact alternative imaginaries of future cybersecurity.

Cleft lip and palate (CL/P) are congenital craniofacial conditions that require coordinated, multidisciplinary care from infancy through growth. Presurgical orthopedic and prosthetic appliances, such as feeding/palatal plates and nasoalveolar molding (NAM) devices, are used in selected patients, and digital workflows based on intraoral or three-dimensional (3D) scanning, computer-aided design and manufacturing (CAD/CAM), and 3D printing are increasingly proposed as alternatives to conventional fabrication. This study was conducted to map the available evidence on conventionally and digitally fabricated prosthetic and presurgical appliances for infants and young children with CL/P, to describe the characteristics of that evidence, and to identify research gaps. A scoping review was conducted and reported according to the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), using a Population–Concept–Context framework. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and Google Scholar were searched. Two reviewers screened records independently. Data were charted using a predefined set of items and summarized descriptively (counts and percentages) and narratively. No formal risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis was undertaken. Thirty sources were included: 7 systematic reviews (3 with meta-analysis), 1 randomized controlled trial, 2 observational clinical studies, 13 case reports, case series, or technical reports, 4 workflow-development or technical-validation studies, 2 in vitro studies, and 1 narrative review. Twenty-three sources (76.7%) were published in 2021 or later. By focus, 10 addressed feeding/palatal plates and obturators, 4 digital impression or scanning, 5 conventional NAM, 9 digital NAM or presurgical plate workflows, and 2 artificial intelligence (AI)-supported planning. Digital workflows were feasible in all categories and offered advantages in data storage, reproducibility, and virtual adjustment. Improved fit was demonstrated mainly in vitro. The only randomized trial in neonates (n = 30) favored digital over tray impressions, whereas a meta-analysis of five randomized trials found no significant differences between digital and conventional NAM in several presurgical outcomes, with low-to-moderate certainty of evidence. Digital workflows redistributed rather than uniformly reduced work time. Digital technology should be regarded as an extension of established clinical practice rather than an automatic substitute for conventional methods. The evidence base is recent, small, and dominated by low-level designs. Future progress depends on standardized digital protocols, larger randomized trials, long-term follow-up, validated materials, and careful integration of AI with clinical expertise.
